c8c4a8568883053e.text: The 👍 that cost $82,000. A grain buyer in Canada texted a farmer a contract. He wrote: “Please confirm flax contract.” The farmer replied with just a 👍. Later, there was a fight about the deal. The farmer said 👍 meant “I got your message”. The buyer said it meant “I agree”. In 2023 a judge said the 👍 meant “I agree”. The farmer had to pay about $82,000. At work, even a tiny reply can count. Think about it. What did 👍 mean to the farmer? What could he have written instead?

395e61814afe8983.text: Turn it up, turn it down. Think of your words like a volume dial. With your mates, you turn it down: short, relaxed, full of in-jokes and emojis. That's casual language. With a boss, a teacher or a stranger at a service desk, you turn it up: full words, a greeting, please and thanks. That's formal language. Neither one is wrong. The trick is choosing the right one. Ask yourself three questions: Who am I talking to? How well do I know them? Are they in charge? Why am I writing? Am I asking for something, saying sorry, or giving information? Where will they read it? A text, an email, a phone call? The less well you know someone, and the more they have a say over you, the more formal you go. A message to your boss about a shift should have a greeting, full words, a clear request and your name at the end. One more thing: short replies count. An emoji or a quick “ok” can be taken as a real answer — so think before you send. Before you hit send, proofread. Read it once more, out loud if you can. Fix spelling, add a greeting, and check it says what you mean.

b34e2945e7e6d8b2.text: The 👍 that cost $82,000. In 2021, a grain buyer in Canada texted a farmer. He sent a photo of a contract to buy flax. He wrote: “Please confirm flax contract.” The farmer replied with one thing: a 👍 thumbs-up emoji. When the flax wasn't delivered, the buyer went to court. The farmer said the thumbs-up only meant he had received the message — not that he agreed. In 2023 a judge ruled that the 👍 did mean “I agree”. The farmer was ordered to pay about $82,000 (Canadian). In 2024, Saskatchewan's Court of Appeal upheld the decision. The lesson: at work, even a tiny reply can be taken seriously. Think about it. What did the farmer think 👍 meant? What did the judge decide? Why might a boss read a short reply differently from a mate? What could the farmer have written instead?

c377edea303a2ba1.text: Turn it up, turn it down. Think of your words like a volume dial. With your mates, you turn it down: short, relaxed, full of in-jokes and emojis. That's casual language. With a boss, a teacher or a stranger at a service desk, you turn it up: full words, a greeting, please and thanks. That's formal language. Neither one is wrong. The trick is choosing the right one. Ask yourself three questions: Who am I talking to? How well do I know them? Are they in charge? Why am I writing? Am I asking for something, saying sorry, or giving information? Where will they read it? A text, an email, a phone call? The less well you know someone, and the more they have a say over you, the more formal you go. Linguists call this choice your register. Your language also shows who you are. Slang can show you belong to a group; formal language can show you're reliable and serious. Switching between them isn't being fake — it's a skill. Short replies count. An emoji or a quick “ok” can be taken as a real answer — so think before you send. And before you hit send, proofread: cut anything repeated, put the most important point first, and check every word.
